title: Embattled Sinaloa Governor Returns and Leaves Office Again (In One Weekend) – Soberanía 121
author: Mexico Solidarity
content:
In episode 121 of Soberanía, hosts José Luis Granados Ceja and Kurt Hackbarth
open with the return and swift departure of Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya,
who briefly reclaimed his office after 112 days on leave — only to face
blistering criticism from President Sheinbaum and his own party. The hosts
unpack the onion-like layers of the Sinaloa case: the bitter university
rivalry between Rocha and his slain rival Héctor Melesio Cuen, the internal
cartel war between the Chapitos and Mayitos the opaque role of the U.S.
government, and the politically timed indictment that conveniently distracted
from the Chihuahua CIA scandal. They argue the U.S. is using the case to
destabilize Mexico ahead of the 2027 midterms.

Next, they examine the collapse of U.S.-Canada trade talks and what it means
for Mexico. With Canada walking away from the negotiating table and imposing
retaliatory tariffs, the hosts see a golden opportunity for Mexico to stand
firm — since the U.S. can't afford a trade war on two fronts. They contrast
Canada's consumer boycott of U.S. products with the Mexican right's slavish
devotion to American imports.

The conversation then returns to the Cerimedo affair, the far-right operative
arrested in Bolivia for allegedly masterminding an assassination attempt on
his pregnant ex-partner. The hosts connect the dots between Cerimedo, Javier
Negre, Ricardo Salinas Pliego, and the wider network of MAGA-linked
consultants — including Brad Parscale and the Miami-based lobbyists who are
paid by Mexican taxpayer dollars to undermine Mexico's own government. They
warn that while Cerimedo may be down, the infrastructure that enabled him
remains intact.

Losers and Haters takes aim at Bloomberg for publishing a video claiming
investors are treating Mexican debt like junk — despite Mexico's strong
economic fundamentals. The hosts argue this is part of a coordinated campaign
to pressure Mexico into privatizing its energy sector, with ratings agencies
serving as weapons of financial blackmail.
